name: Zuluk
tagline: An old mule-train halt on the road to Jelep La, now homestays
meta_description: Zuluk on the Old Silk Route: the zigzag road, Thambi View Point, Lungthung sunrise, Rongli permits, homestay prices and when the snow closes the road.
summary: Zuluk is a small village at about 2,900 m in East Sikkim, once the night halt for mule trains on the Kalimpong–Lhasa road over Jelep La. Today it is the base for the Silk Route drive: the zigzag road from Thambi View Point, sunrise at Lungthung, and family homestays at ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals.

local_story.title: The last night halt before Jelep La
paras: For most of the Raj era, the busiest road between India and Tibet did not run through Gangtok. It ran from Kalimpong to Pedong, Rhenock and Rongli, then climbed through the forest to Zuluk, over Jelep La at 4,390 m and down into the Chumbi valley. The Bengal District Gazetteer explained Jelep La as the lovely level pass. Wool came down it on the backs of mules, bound for Kalimpong's warehouses; cloth, salt, tools and tea went up. Zuluk, at about 2,900 m, was a night halt on that route: the place where muleteers rested animals and men before the long, cold pull to the pass.

The road was also a road of war. In 1888 British troops pushed Tibetan forces back from Lingtu on this ridge, and on 22 May 1888 the two sides clashed at Gnathang, a short drive above Zuluk. Trade went on for decades after. It thinned with the events in Tibet in 1959, and when the border was sealed after 1962 the mule trains stopped for good. Zuluk became what it still is: an army camp with a village around it, cut off by 1–1.5 m of snow in a hard winter.

What brought outsiders back was the road itself. The army highway, now NH717B, climbs above Zuluk in tier after tier of hairpin bends, and once photographs of those loops travelled, families here began to open their homes to guests. Today Zuluk's homestays feed travellers the way the halt once fed muleteers: simply, early to bed, and up before dawn for the climb to Lungthung.

did_you_know: Zuluk, at about 2,900 m (9,400 ft), was a night halt for mule trains on the Kalimpong–Lhasa trade road over Jelep La, used until the events of 1959 in Tibet.
The Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary around Zuluk was set up in 2002 and shelters red panda, Himalayan black bear, blood pheasant, kalij pheasant and Himalayan monal.
On 22 May 1888 British and Tibetan forces clashed at Gnathang, a short drive above Zuluk, during the British expedition that pushed Tibetan troops back from Lingtu.
intro: Zuluk is not a sightseeing town. It is a line of houses, an army camp and a few shops on a shoulder of the hill, with the forest of Pangolakha falling away below and the famous road coiling above. People come for two things: the view of that road from Thambi View Point, about 3,400 m, and the sunrise over Kanchenjunga from Lungthung, about 3,900 m. Both are early-morning trips, which is why we suggest sleeping in Zuluk rather than rushing through from Gangtok in a single long day.

The trip needs some planning. Indian travellers need a Silk Route permit, issued at Rongli, and almost everyone goes up in a reserved car arranged by a homestay or a Gangtok operator. Homestays cost about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast, which keeps the stay itself cheap; the car is the big cost, at roughly ₹5,000–7,000 a day. Nights are cold in every month. From December to February snow can close the road, and from June to September landslides do. Check current status before you travel.
facts: Patchy at best; plan to be offline
costs: Reserved SUV for the Silk Route
Small fee; agent or homestay may charge for arranging it
Thukpa or noodle soup in a village shop
Hired boots or warm coat, winter

highlights.title: Thambi View Point
highlights.text: At about 3,400 m above Zuluk, this is where the photograph comes from: the road below folding back on itself in loop after loop down the hillside. It is best on a clear morning between October and April, before cloud rises from the valleys. Expect it to be cold and windy even in May.

highlights.title: Sunrise from Lungthung
highlights.text: Lungthung, about 3,900 m, faces west across the Sikkim hills to the Kanchenjunga range. Drivers leave Zuluk around 4.30–5 am so you reach it before the first light hits the summit. On a clear October or November morning the snow turns pink, then gold, then white within about twenty minutes.

highlights.title: Pangolakha forest and birds
highlights.text: Zuluk sits within the landscape of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, set up in 2002. Blood pheasant, kalij pheasant and Himalayan monal are seen along the road edges in early morning, and red panda and Himalayan black bear live in the forest, though sightings are rare. Walk slowly and quietly near the bends.

highlights.title: Rhododendrons in April and May
highlights.text: In spring the slopes between Zuluk and Thambi turn red, pink and cream as the rhododendrons flower. This is also the season when the road is usually open, the days are long and the snow has pulled back from the higher bends, which makes late April our favourite time to come.

highlights.title: Winter snow
highlights.text: In a hard winter Zuluk gets 1–1.5 m of snow, and the hairpins above it turn white. It is the reason many Bengal families come in January and February. The cost is uncertainty: the road can close for days, cars need chains, and some homestays shut. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: The road to Gnathang and Kupup
highlights.text: From Zuluk the Silk Route continues past Thambi and Lungthung to the Gnathang valley, the old Baba Mandir and Kupup, where Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake, lies below the Dongkya Range. It makes a full day out and back, or a one-way route towards Gangtok via Tsomgo.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep from Gangtok to Rongli, about 69 km and 2.5–3 h, for ₹200–300 a seat. Get your permit at Rongli, then go up the last 32 km (about 1.5 h) in a car your homestay arranges. This is the cheapest way, but it needs your documents ready and an early start.

how_to_reach.mode: Reserved SUV from Gangtok or Siliguri
how_to_reach.text: Most travellers hire an SUV for the whole Silk Route at about ₹5,000–7,000 a day. The driver or operator arranges the Rongli permit in advance with your photo ID and photos. From Siliguri the drive is about 140–150 km and 5–6 h via Rangpo and Rongli.

When NH10 along the Teesta is shut, as it has often been since the October 2023 flood, cars come up from Siliguri through Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock to Rongli. It is the old trade route and roughly as long. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Zuluk has no hotels in the usual sense. You sleep in the family homestays of Zuluk village: simple rooms in wooden or concrete houses along the road, with thick quilts, shared or attached bathrooms and hot water by the bucket. Dinner and breakfast are part of the rate, usually ₹1,200–2,000 per person, and the food is rice, dal, a vegetable, eggs or chicken, and noodles in the morning. Rooms are cold from October to April, so ask for an extra quilt and carry a warm hat for the night. If Zuluk is full, the homestays of Padamchen lower down or Gnathang higher up are the alternatives.
tips: Carry at least four photocopies of your photo ID and four passport photos per person for the Rongli permit and checkpoints.
Bring enough cash for the whole trip, because there is no ATM you can count on beyond Rongli.
Sleep in Zuluk or Padamchen before going higher, rather than driving straight from Gangtok to Gnathang in one day.
Pack a down jacket, gloves and a warm hat even in May; dawn at Lungthung is below freezing for much of the year.
Ask your homestay about the road the evening before, because snow, landslides and army movement can change plans overnight.

experiences.title: The zigzag loops from Thambi View Point
experiences.cost: Included in your Silk Route car
experiences.summary: A short drive above Zuluk to Thambi View Point, about 3,400 m, where the Silk Route road can be seen below in tier after tier of hairpin bends. Go early on a clear morning, before cloud fills the valley, and dress for wind.
body: Thambi View Point is a roadside platform on the climb from Zuluk towards Lungthung, about 500 m higher than the village. From the edge you look straight down on the road you have just driven: bend over bend, stacked down the hillside, with the army camp and Zuluk's roofs further below. It is the single most photographed view in East Sikkim, and the reason many people come at all. Most drivers stop here on the way down from Lungthung after sunrise, which is the best plan.

Light matters more than anything. Between about 7 and 9 am on a clear day the sun is behind you and the road stands out sharp against the slope. By late morning cloud often rises from the valleys and the loops vanish, sometimes for the rest of the day. In winter the bends can be white with snow, which looks fine in photographs but means the road may be closed, and in the monsoon months you may see nothing at all.

It is cold and windy at 3,400 m in every month, so take a jacket, a hat and gloves out of the car with you. Stay behind the barriers; the edge is steep and the ground can be icy. Tea stalls appear here in the main seasons, but do not count on them. There is no entry fee. The stop is covered by your Silk Route permit and your car hire, and fifteen to thirty minutes is plenty.

faqs.q: How far is Thambi View Point from Zuluk?
faqs.a: Thambi View Point is a short drive above Zuluk on the road towards Lungthung, usually about 30–45 minutes depending on road and snow. It sits at about 3,400 m, some 500 m above the village. Most drivers stop here on the way back from the Lungthung sunrise rather than going up twice.

faqs.q: What is the best time to see the Zuluk loops?
faqs.a: Clear mornings between October and April, roughly 7–9 am, give the sharpest view of the loops. Cloud usually rises by late morning. From June to September the road is often wrapped in mist and landslides can close it, so the view is a gamble then. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Thambi View Point?
faqs.a: No. Thambi View Point is a roadside stop on NH717B and there is no ticket. You do need the Silk Route permit that covers Zuluk and the road beyond, which Indian travellers get at Rongli, usually arranged by the driver or homestay. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sunrise over Kanchenjunga from Lungthung
experiences.cost: Included in your Silk Route car
experiences.summary: A pre-dawn drive from Zuluk to Lungthung, about 3,900 m, to watch the first light reach Kanchenjunga and the snow peaks to the west. On a clear morning the range turns pink, then gold, within twenty minutes. It is cold, early and, on a good day, the best hour of the trip.
body: Lungthung is a small settlement and army post on the Silk Route above Thambi, at about 3,900 m. It faces west across the folded hills of Sikkim to the Kanchenjunga range, and on clear mornings the whole line of snow peaks stands up on the horizon. Drivers based in Zuluk know the drill: they knock on your door around 4–4.30 am, and you leave in the dark so you are in place before the sun rises behind you and lights the summits first.

What you see depends entirely on the weather. October and November give the most reliable clear dawns, with December, March and April close behind. On a good morning the top of Kanchenjunga turns pink, then orange, then white as the light moves down the mountain, and the valleys below stay dark and full of cloud. On a poor morning you see cloud. There is no way to know in advance, which is why we suggest two nights in Zuluk if you can spare them.

Dress for minus temperatures in any month: thermal layers, a down jacket, gloves, a woollen hat and thick socks. Take a flask of tea from your homestay, as stalls at Lungthung may not be open at dawn. Walk slowly at this height and do not run for the best spot. On the way down, stop at Thambi View Point for the loops in morning light, and be back in Zuluk for breakfast by about 8.

faqs.q: What time should we leave Zuluk for the Lungthung sunrise?
faqs.a: Leave Zuluk between about 4.30 and 5 am, a little earlier in summer and a little later in winter. The drive up takes around 45 minutes to an hour, depending on road and snow. Ask your homestay or driver the evening before, because they time it by the season and the weather.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Lungthung?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings the Kanchenjunga range is visible to the west from Lungthung, about 3,900 m. October and November give the best odds, followed by December and the spring months. From June to September cloud usually hides it, and even in good months the view can disappear within an hour or two of sunrise.

faqs.q: Is Lungthung safe for children and older travellers?
faqs.a: At about 3,900 m, Lungthung is high enough to cause headaches and breathlessness, especially if you came straight from the plains. Sleep at Zuluk first, keep children warm, move slowly and drink water. People with heart or lung problems should take medical advice before the trip, and anyone feeling unwell should go down.

experiences.title: Pheasant mornings on the Pangolakha road
experiences.cost: Free on foot · local guide ₹800–1,500 if available
experiences.summary: A slow early walk along the road edges around Zuluk, inside the landscape of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, looking for blood pheasant, kalij pheasant and Himalayan monal. Red panda and black bear live here too, though few visitors see them. Binoculars and patience matter more than distance.
body: The Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary was set up in 2002 and covers about 124 km² of forest and alpine slopes, rising from about 1,760 m to 4,390 m. Zuluk sits within that landscape, and the road around it passes through oak, rhododendron and fir forest that holds some of the Himalaya's best-known birds. Blood pheasant are often seen in small groups on the verges in the early morning. Kalij pheasant keep to lower, thicker cover, and the Himalayan monal, with its metallic colours, prefers open slopes higher up.

There are no trails or hides here. You simply walk a quiet stretch of road at first light, stop often, scan the slopes and listen. March to May is the best season, when birds call and the rhododendrons flower; October and November are good too. Red panda and Himalayan black bear live in the sanctuary, but sightings are rare and you should never go into the forest looking for them. Keep to the road and stay with your group.

Bring binoculars, a warm layer and a field guide or app. Ask your homestay whether anyone in the village guides birders; some families know the birds well, but there is no fixed guide system, so we cannot promise one. Rates, where available, are roughly ₹800–1,500 for a morning. Walk on the hill side of the road, watch for army trucks on the bends, and do not use playback calls on pheasants.

faqs.q: Which birds can you see around Zuluk?
faqs.a: The birds people most hope for around Zuluk are blood pheasant, kalij pheasant and Himalayan monal, all recorded in the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary. Early mornings from March to May give the best chances. You will also see smaller forest birds in mixed flocks. Sightings are never guaranteed, and mist can end a morning early.

faqs.q: Can we see red panda near Zuluk?
faqs.a: Red panda live in the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary around Zuluk, but sightings by visitors are rare. They keep to dense forest and are mostly active at dawn and dusk. Do not leave the road to look for them, and be wary of anyone promising a sighting. Treat a red panda as a lucky bonus.

faqs.q: Do we need a separate permit for birding at Zuluk?
faqs.a: Walking the road near Zuluk is normally covered by the Silk Route permit Indian travellers get at Rongli. Going deep into the sanctuary forest is another matter and may need forest department permission and a local guide. Rules change, so ask at your homestay or the Rongli office and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Up the old trade road to Gnathang and Kupup
experiences.best_time: Oct–Nov and Apr–May; road permitting in winter
experiences.cost: Included in a ₹5,000–7,000 a day SUV
experiences.summary: A full day from Zuluk along the Silk Route past Thambi and Lungthung to the high Gnathang valley, the old Baba Mandir and Kupup, where Bitang Tso lies below the Dongkya Range. It follows the line of the Raj-era trade road towards Jelep La and climbs to about 4,000 m.
body: Beyond Lungthung the road leaves the forest and enters open, high country. The Gnathang valley, at roughly 3,800–4,000 m, is a broad grassy bowl with yak herders, a small monastery and a handful of homestays; the 2011 census counted 13 households and 60 people in Gnathang village. On 22 May 1888 British and Tibetan forces clashed here, and war memorials stand along this stretch of road. It is a quiet place now, and very cold at night.

Further on is the old Baba Mandir, the original bunker shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh of the Punjab Regiment, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit still guards the border; treat that as faith, and respect it. Then comes Kupup, around 3,950–4,000 m, below the Dongkya Range near Jelep La. Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake, is regarded as the source of the Dichu river. Jelep La was the main Kalimpong–Lhasa pass of the Raj era.

Most people make this a day trip from Zuluk, out and back, or continue one way to Gangtok via Baba Mandir and Tsomgo if their permit and car allow. Take it slowly: you gain over 1,000 m from Zuluk, and headaches are common. Carry water, snacks, sun cream and dark glasses, because the snow glare is strong. Snow can close the road from December to April, and landslides can close it in the monsoon. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we go from Zuluk to Gangtok via Kupup and Tsomgo?
faqs.a: Often yes. The Silk Route continues from Zuluk through Gnathang and Kupup to the Nathu La road, then down past Tsomgo to Gangtok. Whether you may do it depends on your permit and on the road being open, and some drivers prefer to return via Rongli. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How high is Kupup and is it safe?
faqs.a: Kupup lies at about 3,950–4,000 m, more than 1,000 m above Zuluk. Healthy adults who slept a night at Zuluk usually manage a short visit, but headaches and breathlessness are common. Do not run, avoid alcohol the night before, keep children warm, and turn back if anyone feels faint, confused or very unwell.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Gnathang?
faqs.a: Yes, Gnathang has a few family homestays and some travellers stay a night there. It is colder than Zuluk, well below freezing on winter nights, and at about 3,800–4,000 m it is a big jump in height. We suggest at least one night at Zuluk or Padamchen first, and sleeping at Gnathang only if everyone is well.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Zuluk?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need a Silk Route permit for Zuluk, Gnathang and Kupup, issued at Rongli. Most people let their homestay or Gangtok driver arrange it in advance, using copies of photo ID and passport photos. Foreigners face different rules, and access for them has varied over the years. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Zuluk from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Zuluk is about 100 km from Gangtok via Rongli, roughly 4–4.5 hours. The cheap way is a shared jeep to Rongli for ₹200–300 a seat, then a car arranged by your homestay for the last 32 km. Most people hire an SUV for the whole Silk Route at about ₹5,000–7,000 a day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Zuluk?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest views of Kanchenjunga and the zigzag road. April and May bring rhododendrons and longer days. December to February brings snow, which is beautiful but can close the road for days. June to September is monsoon, with landslides and cloud, and we suggest avoiding it.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Zuluk?
faqs.a: Foreigners need a Restricted Area Permit to enter Sikkim and a further permit, through a registered agent, for the Silk Route. Access for foreign nationals to Zuluk and the road beyond has changed several times, and rules are sometimes tighter than for Indian travellers. Ask a registered Gangtok agent well ahead and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Zuluk trip cost?
faqs.a: For two people sharing, a two-night Silk Route trip from Gangtok usually costs about ₹14,000–20,000 in all. The car is the biggest share at ₹5,000–7,000 a day; homestays add ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals. Snacks, tea and permit charges are small extras. Shared jeeps to Rongli cut costs for solo travellers.

faqs.q: Does it snow in Zuluk?
faqs.a: Yes. Zuluk usually gets snow between December and February, and in a hard winter the fall can reach 1–1.5 m. The higher road towards Thambi, Lungthung and Gnathang sees snow more often and for longer, sometimes into April. Snow can close the road, so keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do we need for Zuluk and the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Two nights is the comfortable minimum: one in Zuluk to rest and adjust, then a dawn trip to Lungthung and a day to Gnathang and Kupup. Three nights lets you add Padamchen or a night at Gnathang. A single rushed night works, but leaves no room for bad weather or road closures.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and an ATM in Zuluk?
faqs.a: Mobile signal in Zuluk is patchy and can vanish for hours, so plan to be offline and share your plans with family before you leave Rongli. There is no ATM we would rely on beyond Rongli. Carry cash for homestays, food, tips and any permit charges, plus a little extra for a delay.

faqs.q: Is Zuluk suitable for children and senior citizens?
faqs.a: Zuluk itself, at about 2,900 m, suits most healthy families and older travellers who go slowly. The day trips climb to 3,400–4,000 m, which is harder. Keep children warm and hydrated, avoid the trip with infants, and take medical advice for anyone with heart or lung conditions. Turn back if anyone feels unwell.
